title: E29 - Why Firms Are Buying Niche AI, Centari Founder Kevin Walker
author: Kevin Walker

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source shifts the emphasis from end-to-end delivery redesign, pricing pressure and apprenticeship toward sophisticated firms’ enduring role in navigating complexity and converting proprietary expertise into structured, AI-usable knowledge. It acknowledges commoditised work moving in-house, but presents differentiated knowledge infrastructure—not workflow automation—as the central strategic response.
qs: And I think a lot of work is shifting in-house for what's, you know, in some cases described as commoditized work.
But the most critical layer of the cake is that knowledge is that expertise in a structured format that attorneys and AI tools can act upon to deliver unique client value.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not address whether automation of junior work threatens apprenticeship, creates a verification-experience paradox, or requires reconstructed training. It instead focuses on high-fidelity firm data, current AI drafting limitations and preserving lawyers’ advisory role amid business complexity.
qs: It's still not drafting a stock purchase agreement with the quality of a seventh year associate.

And what Centari is doing is helping these firms aggregate their knowledge, aggregate this information in a way that helps them deliver that next level of insight and knowledge through the complexity.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Walker accepts the cluster’s selective-insourcing proposition by observing that commoditized work is moving in-house, while materially extending it with a law-firm response: structure proprietary knowledge and expertise so firms can preserve differentiated value through AI-enabled services rather than compete on routine work.
qs: And I think a lot of work is shifting in-house for what's, you know, in some cases described as commoditized work.
But the most critical layer of the cake is that knowledge is that expertise in a structured format that attorneys and AI tools can act upon to deliver unique client value.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source accepts that generative AI makes complex, unstructured legal text tractable and supports specialist value through a concrete structured-data layer for transactional documents. It materially extends the cluster by distinguishing this information-access model from the predominant lawyer-facing copilot model, rather than rejecting workflow augmentation altogether.
qs: And what I mean by that is when you have a technology that can take vast amounts of textual data, unstructured data, and create structure from that information, create structure from complex merger agreements, complex credit agreements for enterprise, you know, all their vendor contracts.

It's a very different direction as a company than, let's go build an AI assistant, let's go build a co-pilot for lawyers, which is how many of these products were framed in the early days and I think still are building in that direction.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Walker accepts that AI will automate commodity production while lawyers and firms retain value through specialized judgment and guidance. He materially extends the cluster by arguing that structured, proprietary firm knowledge is the critical data layer that will improve AI outputs and differentiate providers.
qs: But the most critical layer of the cake is that knowledge is that expertise in a structured format that attorneys and AI tools can act upon to deliver unique client value.
And that complexity is not going to be, it's not going away with AI augmented attorney workflows.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-centred deployment and materially develops the cluster’s operating-model thesis. It argues that complex transactional work requires specialised orchestration rather than an off-the-shelf model, and identifies firm-specific structured knowledge as the critical infrastructure through which lawyers and downstream AI can deliver value. It also reinforces that AI automates commodity work without displacing lawyers’ role in navigating business complexity.
qs: It's hard for a model, too, so it makes sense that this is not a task that an off-the-shelf LLM can perform at an attorney standard.
But the most critical layer of the cake is that knowledge is that expertise in a structured format that attorneys and AI tools can act upon to deliver unique client value.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: Walker directly supports the cluster’s user-led framing by treating live deployment, actual use and customer value—not AI branding or publicity—as the core measures of success. His remarks state strategic criteria rather than providing measured evidence that these criteria produce successful adoption or outcomes.
qs: But within reason, I think the real measure of success is are we deployed live with customers?

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition by presenting legal AI as specialised deal infrastructure rather than a general-purpose assistant and by treating isolated deployments and enterprise security as prerequisites for handling sensitive transaction data. Its claims are vendor self-reports and do not establish verified gains in service quality, productivity or legal outcomes.
qs: We say, we're not building the productivity suite, we're not building the AI assistant.
So single tenant deploys, getting our SOC 2 type 2, everything that is table stakes for serving this class of customers.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of diverse competition by presenting Centari’s specialised deal-intelligence niche as a viable alternative to general-purpose legal AI. However, its claim that Centari is doing well is qualitative and provides no evidence of durable returns, broad adoption or market displacement.
qs: Now, this may seem like a very niche use case, but Centari is doing really well, and they're sparking a more general conversation about the role of general applications versus niche solutions.
They are doing something very specific, deal intelligence.

kp.k: Deal intelligence structures previously inaccessible transactional knowledge
kp.d: Walker distinguishes AI-enabled access to information from workflow augmentation through lawyer assistants. He describes Centari's initial product as converting merger agreements, credit agreements and limited partnership agreements into structured deal data, primarily for large law firms, enabling precedent retrieval and analysis of accumulated transactional knowledge.
qs: So you have sort of the work augmentation path and you have the access to information path.
We were thinking, how can we take complex information that is buried in unstructured text and turn that into structured data that we can deliver to end users when and where they need it.

kp.k: Walker claims substantial acceleration of complex agreement analysis
kp.d: Walker claims Centari can turn answering 200 complex, highly negotiated deal-point questions about a 300-page credit agreement from an attorney's 8 to 10 hours of manual work into a 5 to 10-minute workflow. This is a vendor-reported performance claim; the discussion supplies no independent testing, accuracy results or specified human verification requirements.
qs: This is, let's take a set of 200 very complex questions, very highly negotiated deal points for a 300-page credit agreement, for example, where it would take an attorney 8 to 10 hours to review that agreement and answer each of those questions manually. We're accelerating that into a 5 to 10-minute workflow.

kp.k: Aggregated deal data can reveal negotiating patterns
kp.d: Walker says structured data supports both finding particular precedents and generating insights across a firm's transactions. His hypothetical example is a healthcare M&A leader structuring its previous 10 years of deals to identify market trends and counterparties' negotiation positions; it is not a reported customer study.
qs: In the aggregate, you can start to see trends, you can start to see negotiation positions of particular counterparties, and that becomes a source of insight for the attorneys.

kp.k: Knowledge-based value may align adoption incentives better than efficiency
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that adoption is attractive when AI unlocks valuable capabilities and aligns with the incentives of firms and their lawyers. He contrasts market knowledge that strengthens negotiating authority with speed improvements that may reduce billable hours, while explicitly acknowledging that the hourly-billing incentive problem is often overstated. His market-maker framing is an argument, not demonstrated market impact.
qs: And I'm using this example because it's one that people go to often, and I know it's overstated, but the incentive problem is certainly there.

They want to be able to say like, no, no, no, no, it's not that you're asking for something that's unreasonable. You're saying, listen, we know the market, and in fact, we almost set and make the market.

kp.k: Commoditized work shifts in-house as outside counsel differentiate
kp.d: Drawing on his experience as in-house counsel, Walker argues that clients pay premium outside-counsel rates for distinctive knowledge rather than documents alone. He says in-house lawyers can increasingly generate work such as NDAs and master services agreements, and believes more commoditized work is shifting in-house while firms' future value lies in non-commodity expertise. These are practitioner observations and predictions without quantified market evidence.
qs: Why are we paying the thousand dollar an hour plus rates? It's because we're relying on outside council for that unique insight.
And I think a lot of work is shifting in-house for what's, you know, in some cases described as commoditized work.
And I think increasingly firms are recognizing that the future looks like everything that's non-commodity.

kp.k: Firm-specific data can complement general AI platforms
kp.d: Walker positions Centari as a complementary data layer rather than a replacement for broad legal AI productivity products. Its structured intellectual capital could support attorneys directly or feed downstream AI models and platforms. He argues that proprietary knowledge remains a basis for differentiation even when generative AI tools become widely available.
qs: plug in that data layer into their general AI productivity suite.
Now that everyone has generative AI, everyone's got gen AI, but what is unique about us? It's our unique knowledge, our unique insight, our intellectual capital.

kp.k: Separate deployments protect firms' proprietary deal knowledge
kp.d: Responding to Abramowitz's concern that supplying funds might erode law firms' informational advantage, Walker says each large-firm deployment is single tenant, with a separate server and no commingling of firms' data. He distinguishes those firm-specific datasets from Centari's underlying deal-reasoning technology, which he sees as potentially useful across complex transactions beyond law firms; he does not establish actual adoption by funds.
qs: We do single tenant deployments with large firms.
So it's not commingled with any other law firm data. They have their own walled garden.
The core engine we built, we view as potentially being transformative for deal making more widely.

kp.k: Enterprise security and orchestration underpin the specialized product
kp.d: Walker describes parallel early engineering investments in enterprise infrastructure, including single-tenant deployment and SOC 2 type 2, and a proprietary deal-reasoning orchestration pipeline. He argues that off-the-shelf models cannot perform the described complex extraction at attorney standard without this additional infrastructure. These are vendor explanations rather than comparative evaluation findings.
qs: So single tenant deploys, getting our SOC 2 type 2, everything that is table stakes for serving this class of customers.
While a lot of folks were playing with rag, we went straight into orchestration and realized that that was the way to deliver high fidelity outputs.
this is not a task that an off-the-shelf LLM can perform at an attorney standard.

kp.k: Successful adoption requires innovation, IT and practice alignment
kp.d: Walker reports variable buying routes, including partners, knowledge and innovation teams, and marketing or business-development teams interested in RFPs and client market reports. He recommends involving knowledge and innovation, IT and practicing lawyers from the outset so evaluation, integration and eventual partner and associate usage reinforce one another. This is his implementation advice based on experience, not a systematic adoption study.
qs: Often firms get excited about Centari for producing RFPs and sort of client market reports.
the ones that have successfully triangulated their own stakeholders, which is knowledge and innovation, IT and the practice.
How are you going to drive usage and adoption by the partners and their associates?

kp.k: Automation may increase demand for specialized outside counsel
kp.d: Walker agrees with Abramowitz's proposed specialization trend, reporting that clients increasingly expect commodity services to be automated and seek outside counsel for distinctive market knowledge. He argues that firms retain an advantage because they see a cross-section of transactions that individual clients do not. The claimed direction of change is supported by Walker's reported conversations, not quantified client research.
qs: When we talk to the clients, they are increasingly telling us they just expect so much more to be automated.
We see where the market is moving, which is specialization, unique knowledge.
as a client, you're not doing enough deals to have a sense of the market. You were doing your deals.

kp.k: Fried Frank illustrates the strategic data-layer thesis
kp.d: Abramowitz reports that Fried Frank has gone live with Centari and frames its real-estate expertise as an example of potential market differentiation. Walker confirms the partnership and shared emphasis on a strategic data layer, but offers no usage measures or demonstrated competitive outcomes. The host's suggestion that the firm could effectively own its market should therefore remain distinct from the reported deployment.
qs: shared vision, really, really cool program that he's built at Fried Frank.
we sort of have this, this shared thesis for, you know, starts with the data, got to have that strategic data layer

kp.k: AI purchasing can reflect talent retention and competitive signaling
kp.d: Walker describes purchases driven partly by imitation and pressure to appear AI-enabled rather than a defined problem. Abramowitz argues that such spending may nevertheless be rational insurance against attorney churn, giving an illustrative million or two million dollars annually rather than a documented expenditure. Both also regard enterprise ChatGPT licenses as potentially useful broad entry points; neither supplies comparative procurement results.
qs: the products are being purchased, not to solve a particular problem, but because it's like everyone else is buying it, we got to buy it too.
it's worth it for me to spend a million, two million a year just as a sort of protection policy against like attorney churn.
I think a lot of firms would be well-suited to purchase enterprise chat GBT license, and I think that would get them really far as well.

kp.k: Disappointing first-wave adoption creates demand for better data
kp.d: Walker accepts the host's description of Centari as a second-wave product: after purchasing broad AI tools, firms recognize the importance of high-fidelity data for useful outputs. He describes disappointment with usage and drafting capabilities, including failure to match a seventh-year associate's stock purchase agreement drafting. These are qualitative market observations, not measured adoption rates or a drafting benchmark.
qs: they need to have a high fidelity set of data to act upon for the outputs to be good, for the value to be clear to attorneys.
It's still not drafting a stock purchase agreement with the quality of a seventh year associate.

kp.k: Complex advisory work persists beyond automated document production
kp.d: Walker argues that sophisticated firms help businesses navigate negotiations, regulation, environmental implications and investment structures, rather than merely draft contracts. His thesis is that AI-augmented workflows do not remove this underlying economic complexity, while aggregated institutional knowledge can improve firms' advisory capabilities. This is a conceptual argument for continuing demand, not an employment forecast supported by labor-market data.
qs: lawyers are so much more than the service providers who draft contracts for you.
And that complexity is not going to be, it's not going away with AI augmented attorney workflows.
where a sophisticated law firm sits in the economy is being your guide through that complexity.

kp.k: Harvey discussion separates brand effects from unverified allegations
kp.d: Abramowitz introduces an anonymous Reddit post by someone claiming to be a recently fired Harvey employee and explicitly frames the discussion as speculative. Walker interprets the criticism as a possible consequence of rapid organizational scaling, rather than evidence about product value. Separately, Abramowitz reports anecdotal conversations suggesting Harvey's strong brand can attract buyers or push them toward rivals. Neither the allegations nor their proposed causes are established by the transcript.
qs: Someone went on yesterday claiming to be a recently fired Harvey employee
So what is all this is in the hot take zone.
Maybe we should have like a flashing reckless speculation
Harvey's brand is so strong in a certain sense that it is like influencing purchases on both sides, pro and sort of anti Harvey.

kp.k: Customer deployment and value matter more than fundraising visibility
kp.d: Walker recommends judging a legal AI business by live deployment, actual usage, customer value and continued technical progress rather than publicity or funding announcements. This provides his proposed success criteria, not evidence that those criteria have been met at any specified scale.
qs: the real measure of success is are we deployed live with customers? Are they using the product? Are they seeing value? Are we staying ahead of the curve with the tech we're building? These are the things that matter.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kevin Walker distinguishes AI-enabled access to institutional knowledge from workflow augmentation and claims Centari substantially accelerates complex deal-point extraction.
pts.d: Walker describes two complementary directions for AI: assisting professional work and converting previously inaccessible unstructured information into usable structured data. He says Centari's current deal-intelligence product turns law firms' transactional repositories into searchable deal points, precedents and aggregate insights, including counterparty negotiation patterns. His concrete performance claim is that answering approximately 200 complex questions about a 300-page credit agreement moves from 8–10 hours of manual attorney work to a 5–10-minute workflow. This is a founder-reported capability, not a claim that lawyers are replaced or that complete transactional work is automated.

pts.k: Walker predicts that automation and in-house production of commodity work will increase the importance of specialized knowledge as law firms' source of value.
pts.d: Walker says in-house lawyers can already generate substantial legal work product, with some commoditized work shifting in-house. He predicts that clients will increasingly choose outside counsel for distinctive market knowledge rather than generic drafting. Structured proprietary deal data can strengthen that differentiation and support downstream AI tools. He endorses a direction toward specialization, but does not establish that particular firms will dominate particular markets.

pts.k: Walker claims proprietary data infrastructure is a complementary 'second wave' of legal AI, while current general tools have not eliminated sophisticated firms' role.
pts.d: Walker reports disappointment with adoption and output quality after purchases of first-wave AI platforms. He argues that useful outputs require high-fidelity data and that ubiquitous access to generative AI makes firms' own knowledge and people more important differentiators. He also maintains that AI-augmented workflows do not remove the economic, regulatory and transactional complexity through which sophisticated firms guide clients. His position is complementary to AI productivity platforms, not a prediction of wholesale lawyer substitution.

pts.k: Walker argues that legal-AI adoption depends on organizational coordination, security and specialized engineering, and sees potential beyond law firms.
pts.d: Walker says successful firm adoption requires alignment among knowledge and innovation teams, IT and practicing lawyers. For sensitive transactional data, he describes enterprise security and single-tenant deployment as prerequisites to serving large firms. He says off-the-shelf LLMs cannot perform the demanding extraction task at attorney standard without a sophisticated pipeline and orchestration. He also sees Centari's underlying engine as potentially transformative for complex dealmaking outside law firms, while emphasizing that each firm's extracted data remains separate. Separately, he acknowledges that some AI purchases are driven by talent competition and client-facing innovation positioning rather than a specific operational problem.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest mainly on Walker's legal experience, customer conversations and founder-reported product development and deployments.
pts.d: Walker draws on his experience as a Paul Hastings M&A lawyer, startup GC and deputy GC at a private-equity fund to explain demand for outside counsel's market knowledge. He cites conversations with clients about expected automation and observations of firms' adoption processes. Fried Frank is a named partnership illustrating the strategic-data thesis, but Walker supplies no measured customer outcomes. The extraction-speed comparison is not accompanied by a benchmark methodology, sample size, accuracy results or an account of human verification time. Claims about off-the-shelf model limitations and orchestration derive from his description of Centari's R&D, without comparative test results. Specialization and wider dealmaking transformation are presented as the company's thesis and expectations rather than demonstrated market-wide findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Walker mixes present-tense product and adoption claims in the 2025 interview with longer-term predictions that have no fixed deadline.
pts.d: Extraction acceleration, in-house movement of commodity work and disappointment with first-wave tools are described as current developments. Specialization, proprietary-data differentiation and expansion into broader dealmaking are directional forecasts without dates. Aggregate insights depend on access to a sufficiently rich body of past transactions; Walker's ten-year healthcare M&A example is illustrative, not a study period. Deployment success is conditional on integration, practice buy-in and ongoing usage, and sensitive firm data is described as remaining within firm-specific deployments. His reassurance about firms is explicitly qualified as 'right now at least.' No quantified timetable for job losses, changes in staffing or elimination of firms is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are large transactional firms, their lawyers and implementation teams, and corporate or financial-services clients.
pts.d: Large firms are positioned to turn accumulated transaction histories into reusable intellectual capital and differentiated advice. Partners and associates gain faster access to precedents, negotiated terms and aggregate market information; marketing and business-development teams can use it for RFPs and client market reports. Knowledge and innovation staff, IT leaders and developers, and practice teams share responsibility for purchasing, integration and adoption. In-house counsel can retain more commodity production while seeking specialist outside insight. Funds and other financial-services professionals are potential users of the underlying technology, but Walker argues individual clients usually lack the cross-client transaction coverage of outside counsel. Centari is described as a software provider, not an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work. The interview makes no concrete access-to-justice or public-facing legal-service prediction.
